paragraphs: Propaganda plays were staged at the Erode conference. One was M. R. Radha's; another was my own Thooku Medai, which I had written and in which I acted. Including the musicians, twenty of us had to travel from Tiruvarur to Erode. Since Periyar himself was directly looking after conference arrangements, he sent eighty rupees toward our travel expenses. It was not enough, so we each added a little and reached Erode.

After the conference we had to return home, and that again required money. Only Periyar could provide it. Once the conference ended, Periyar knew that everyone would come asking for money and stayed out of sight. Somehow I managed to meet him and explain. "Does one play cost so much?" he asked, but gave another fifty rupees. Again we each contributed a little and returned to Tiruvarur. This was another example of Periyar's thrift.

After the Erode conference Anna began trying somehow to save Alagiri. He brought him to Madras and consulted doctors. Alagiri was admitted to the tuberculosis hospital at Tambaram. Anna announced that whenever anyone invited him to a meeting, he would agree only if they first sent at least one hundred rupees to Alagiri's family for treatment and sent him the receipt. Many comrades responded. Even so, the Tambaram hospital eventually gave up on Alagiri. There was no option but to send him home.

Anna came to the railway station to see him off. Alagiri, bedridden, was lifted into the train. When he saw Anna, his eyes filled. Looking at Mathiazhagan standing nearby, he cried: "Tell Anna—tell him that Alagiri now understands who his friends are and who his enemies are." Before falling ill, Alagiri had often attacked Anna in speeches and among friends. Anna, whenever he heard of those attacks and mockery, would only smile; he neither became angry nor answered.

Remembering that generosity—the man he had criticized running to help him the moment he fell ill—Alagiri wept. Anna gave him the one thousand rupees still left from the Chengalpattu district Self-Respect conference fund. Alagiri received it lying down. The train moved off. Anna wiped his eyes and returned from the station.

Alagiri reached Thanjavur and remained bedridden for many days. He died on 28 March 1949. I was in Tiruvarur when the news came. I had a high fever, but on hearing it the fever seemed to fly away. I rushed to Thanjavur. With tens of thousands surrounding him, the great warrior Alagiri made his final journey. A memorial was later built at his burial place.

A few days afterward a students' conference was held at the Karandai Tamil Sangam in Thanjavur. Professor Anbazhagan, comrade Janarthanam and I took part. I unveiled Alagiri's portrait and, speaking out of undying affection, said with some pain that he had not been properly cared for in his final days. I poured out the hurt in my heart without concealment. Anbazhagan too spoke rather sharply.

Periyar, then running a student training camp in a garden belonging to Mavur Sharma, heard about our speeches. He prepared a statement saying that Anbazhagan and I should no longer be invited to meetings, and explaining that Anna had instigated us to speak against him. He ordered it published immediately in Viduthalai and sent N. V. Natarajan to Madras with it. Natarajan argued at length, but Periyar would not yield. The statement shocked me. I gave no reply. Dravidar Kazhagam comrades stopped inviting us.

Meanwhile, through Anna's determined efforts and the tireless work of many of us, and with support from people such as Yathartham Ponnusami Pillai, a cultural programme by Kalaivanar N. S. Krishnan was arranged in Thanjavur for Alagiri's family fund. Together with the two thousand rupees Kalaivanar himself gave, the total fund reached six thousand rupees—a very large sum then.

On 14 May that same year, Rajaji, then Governor-General of India, went to Tiruvannamalai. Periyar met him there and the two spoke privately for a long time. The meeting caused great excitement in Tamil Nadu. It was a time when the Brahmin–non-Brahmin struggle was described as Rajaji at one pole and Periyar at the other. Party comrades waited for details. Periyar released not even a brief note.

Around then a Muthamizh conference was held in Coimbatore, with the scientist G. D. Naidu taking a major part. Periyar and Anna both attended, though their bitterness had grown to the point that they scarcely spoke to each other. Speaking before Periyar, Anna said the country was eager to know what Periyar and Rajaji had discussed at Tiruvannamalai and asked him to explain it at the conference. Periyar replied heatedly that it was entirely his personal matter and could not be disclosed there.

In a later statement Periyar said he had spoken to Rajaji about arranging a successor. In another, he wrote that it had become urgent and necessary to create a legal successor for himself and his property; that he had known and trusted Maniammai for five or six years and believed she had genuine concern for his welfare and that of the movement; and that he intended to make her his heir and, with four or five others, create a trust deed for the movement's functioning and protection of property.

He added that if, for legal validity, certain words had to be used against their preference, no one should imagine that the movement's principles had therefore been lost. Everyone understood the significance of the phrase "for legal validity." In the memoir's interpretation, it meant that Periyar intended to marry Maniammai.

K. K. Neelamegam of Kumbakonam, N. V. N., and S. Gurusami went to Periyar's house at Yercaud and pleaded with him to abandon the arrangement. He refused. Later, following Anna's advice, a delegation consisting of Kanchi Manimozhiyar, T. M. Parthasarathi, Kannabiran and C. V. Rasan also went to Yercaud. Periyar rejected their respectful request as well and said the marriage would take place.

The prospect shocked the Dravidar Kazhagam cadres deeply. Most members of the executive committee wrote condemning the marriage arrangement. Frontline workers surrounded Anna in tears; Anna did not know what to do. Despite everything, the marriage took place on 9 July 1949. Unaware that it had already happened, the Dravidar Kazhagam executive committee met in Tiruchirappalli on the morning of 10 July to discuss the issue. Thirty-two of its forty-six members attended.
